prompt: There are two clocks in Cathy's room. One of them is 25 minutes behind. Now it is showing 7:40. The second clock is 15 minutes ahead. What is the second clock showing now?

solutions.title: Find the real time first
solutions.body:
The first clock is 25 minutes behind, so the real time is 25 minutes later than 7:40: **8:05**. The second clock is 15 minutes ahead of the real time: 8:05 + 15 minutes = **8:20**.

**Answer: (E) 8:20**

solutions.title: Difference between the clocks
solutions.body:
The second clock is $25 + 15 = 40$ minutes ahead of the first clock. 7:40 + 40 minutes = 8:20.

**Answer: (E) 8:20**

prompt: In four of the five pictures, the white area is equal to the grey area. In which picture are the white area and the grey area different?

solutions.title: Look at the dots
solutions.body:
In each square the big grey and white parts without the dots are exactly half each. Now look at the small dots:

- (A) and (C): one grey dot sits on white and one white dot sits on grey — they cancel out.
- (B) and (E): no dots, grey and white are equal.
- (D): **both** dots are grey and both sit on white parts, so grey gets bigger.

**Answer: (D)**

solutions.title: Swap the dots
solutions.body:
Imagine swapping a white dot with a grey dot of the same size. In (A) and (C) that makes the dots disappear into their background and the halves stay equal. In (D) there is no white dot to swap with, so the grey area is two dots bigger than the white area.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: Father hangs the laundry outside on a clothesline. He wants to use as few pegs as possible. For three towels he needs four pegs, as shown. How many pegs does he need for eleven towels?

solutions.title: Neighbours share a peg
solutions.body:
Two neighbouring towels share a peg. There is one peg at the very start and one more peg at the right end of every towel: $1 + 11 = 12$.

**Answer: (B) 12**

solutions.title: Pattern
solutions.body:
1 towel → 2 pegs, 2 towels → 3 pegs, 3 towels → 4 pegs: always one peg more than towels. 11 towels → 12 pegs.

**Answer: (B) 12**

prompt: A math class lasts 45 minutes. Peter can solve any problem from the textbook in exactly 6 minutes. However, he needs one minute rest after solving each problem. How many problems can Peter solve completely during one math class?

solutions.title: Blocks of 7 minutes
solutions.body:
One problem plus its rest takes $6 + 1 = 7$ minutes. After 6 problems and 6 rests, $6 \times 7 = 42$ minutes have passed. Only 3 minutes are left — not enough for a 7th problem.

**Answer: (D) 6**

solutions.title: Check 7 problems
solutions.body:
7 problems need $7 \times 6 = 42$ minutes of work plus 6 rests in between: 48 minutes — more than 45. 6 problems need $36 + 5 = 41$ minutes, which fits.

**Answer: (D) 6**

prompt: Fifteen children are playing hide and seek. One of them is the "seeker". After a while seven children were still hiding. How many children have already been found?

solutions.title: Subtract the seeker
solutions.body:
$15 - 1 = 14$ children hide. 7 are still hiding, so $14 - 7 = 7$ have been found.

**Answer: (D) 7**

solutions.title: Add up
solutions.body:
Seeker + still hiding + found = 15: $1 + 7 + ? = 15$, so $? = 7$.

**Answer: (D) 7**

prompt: Mike and Jake were playing darts. Each one threw three darts (see the picture). Who won, and by how many points did he win?
A regular rectangular pattern on a wall was created with two kinds of tiles: grey and striped. Some tiles have fallen off the wall (see the picture). How many grey tiles have fallen off?

solutions.title: Continue the checkerboard
solutions.body:
Grey and striped tiles alternate in each row and column. Fill in the hole row by row (the wall is 8 tiles long):

- Row 2: 4 tiles missing: grey, striped, grey, striped → 2 grey.
- Row 3: 5 tiles missing: grey, striped, grey, striped, grey → 3 grey.
- Row 4: 6 tiles missing: grey, striped, grey, striped, grey, striped → 3 grey.

$2 + 3 + 3 = 8$.

**Answer: (B) 8**

solutions.title: Count all and subtract
solutions.body:
The wall has $8 \times 5 = 40$ tiles, half of them, 20, grey. Grey tiles still on the wall: 4 in the top row, 4 in the bottom row, 2 in row 2, 1 in row 3, 1 in row 4 → 12. So $20 - 12 = 8$ fell off.

**Answer: (B) 8**

prompt: The year 2012 is a leap year, that means there are 29 days in February. On the 15th of March 2012, the ducklings of my grandfather are 20 days old. When did they hatch from their eggs?

solutions.title: Count back
solutions.body:
15 days back from 15 March brings us to 29 February (the last day of February). We still need $20 - 15 = 5$ more days back: $29 - 5 = 24$, so **24 February**.

**Answer: (D)**

solutions.title: Check forwards
solutions.body:
From 24 February to 29 February is 5 days, and from 29 February to 15 March is 15 days: $5 + 15 = 20$. ✓

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: You have L-shaped tiles, each consisting of four squares as shown. How many of the following shapes can you make by glueing together two of the given tiles?

Once Little Piggy planted 8 acorns. In a few years, oak trees grew from all acorns except two of them. All oak trees except two of them had their acorns. Acorns from all prolific trees except one, are very tasty. How many oaks with tasty acorns are there?

solutions.title: Step by step
solutions.body:
- Oak trees: $8 - 2 = 6$.
- Trees with acorns: $6 - 2 = 4$.
- Trees with tasty acorns: $4 - 1 = 3$.

**Answer: (B) 3**

solutions.title: Take away all the exceptions
solutions.body:
Starting from 8, the story takes away 2, then 2, then 1: $8 - 5 = 3$.

**Answer: (B) 3**

prompt: In a sudoku the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4 can occur only once in each column and once in each row. In the mathematical sudoku on the picture, Patrick first writes in the results of the calculations. Then he completes the sudoku. Which number will Patrick put in the grey cell?

Grandmother made 20 gingerbread biscuits for her grandchildren. She decorated them with raisins and nuts. First she decorated 15 biscuits with raisins and then 15 biscuits with nuts. At least how many biscuits were decorated both with raisins and nuts?
Among Nikolay's classmates there are twice as many girls as there are boys. Which of the following numbers may be equal to the number of all children in this class?

In the animal's school, three kittens, four ducklings, two goslings and several lambs are taking lessons. The teacher owl found out that all of her pupils have 44 legs altogether. How many lambs are among them?

solutions.title: Subtract the known legs
solutions.body:
Kittens: $3 \times 4 = 12$. Ducklings: $4 \times 2 = 8$. Goslings: $2 \times 2 = 4$. Together 24 legs. The lambs have $44 - 24 = 20$ legs, so there are $20 \div 4 = 5$ lambs.

**Answer: (B) 5**

prompt: In one kangaroo family, there is a custom to name their babies by names, which consist of two letters of the word KANGAROO: the first letter is a consonant, the second letter is a vowel. How many different baby names can be composed?

solutions.title: Choices for each letter
solutions.body:
Different consonants in KANGAROO: K, N, G, R (4). Different vowels: A, O (2). Each consonant can go with each vowel: $4 \times 2 = 8$ names.

**Answer: (A) 8**

solutions.title: List them
solutions.body:
KA, KO, NA, NO, GA, GO, RA, RO — 8 names.

**Answer: (A) 8**

prompt: At a Christmas party, there was exactly one candlestick on each of the 15 tables. There were six five-branched candlesticks, and the rest were three-branched ones. How many candles had to be bought for all the candlesticks?

The figure consists of an equilateral triangle, a square and a regular pentagon. It is built by sticks of equal length. At most how many such figures can be built with a box of 2012 sticks of equal length?

solutions.title: Count the sticks in one figure
solutions.body:
Triangle 3 + square 4 + pentagon 5 = 12 sides, but the triangle and the square share one stick and the square and the pentagon share one stick. So one figure needs $12 - 2 = 10$ sticks.

$2012 \div 10 = 201$ with 2 sticks left over.

**Answer: (D) 201**

solutions.title: Count directly
solutions.body:
Look at the picture: the triangle has 2 sticks of its own, the square has 4 sticks (top and bottom are shared but we count them once), the pentagon has 4 sticks of its own. $2 + 4 + 4 = 10$ sticks. 201 figures use 2010 sticks; 202 figures would need 2020.

**Answer: (D) 201**

prompt: Gregor forms two numbers with the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. Both numbers have three digits, and each digit is used only once. Gregor adds these two numbers. What is the greatest sum Gregor can obtain?

Laura, Iggy, Val and Kate want to be in one photo together. Kate and Laura are best friends and they want to stand next to each other. Iggy wants to stand next to Laura because he likes her. In how many possible ways can they arrange for the photo?

A grasshopper wants to climb a staircase with many steps. She can make only two kinds of jumps: three steps up, or four steps down. Beginning at the ground level, at least how many jumps will she have to make in order to take a rest on the 22nd step?

solutions.title: Up jumps minus down jumps
solutions.body:
We need $3 \times (\text{up}) - 4 \times (\text{down}) = 22$.

- 0 down jumps: 22 is not a multiple of 3.
- 1 down jump: up jumps must make 26 — not a multiple of 3.
- 2 down jumps: up jumps must make 30 = 10 jumps of 3. ✓

$10 + 2 = 12$ jumps, e.g. up to 30 in 10 jumps, then down to 26 and 22.

**Answer: (D) 12**

solutions.title: Why not fewer?
solutions.body:
Every up jump lands on a multiple of 3 if there are no down jumps: 21, 24 — never 22. With one down jump we would need to be at 26 before it, which is also not a multiple of 3. So at least 2 down jumps, which means reaching 30 first: 10 up jumps. Total 12.

**Answer: (D) 12**

prompt: Frank made a domino snake of seven tiles. He put the tiles next to each other so that the sides with the same number of dots touched. Originally the snake had 33 dots on its back. However, Frank's brother George took away two tiles from the snake (see the picture). How many dots were in the place with the question mark?

A special clock has three hands of different length (for hours, for minutes, and for seconds). We do not know which hand is which, but we do know that the clock runs correctly. At 12:55:30 p.m. the hands were in the position depicted on the right. How will this clock look at 8:11:00 p.m.?

A rectangular paper sheet measures 192 × 84 mm. You cut the sheet along just one straight line to get two parts, one of which is a square. Then you do the same with the non-square part of the sheet, and so on. What is the length of the side of the smallest square you can get with this procedure?

solutions.title: Cut step by step
solutions.body:
- 192 × 84: cut an 84 × 84 square → 108 × 84.
- 108 × 84: cut 84 × 84 → 24 × 84.
- 24 × 84: cut three 24 × 24 squares → 24 × 12.
- 24 × 12: cut 12 × 12 → 12 × 12, a square.

The smallest square has side 12 mm.

**Answer: (E) 12 mm**

solutions.title: Common measure
solutions.body:
Every cut takes the short side away from the long side, so all lengths stay multiples of every number that divides both 192 and 84. The biggest such number is 12 ($192 = 16 \times 12$, $84 = 7 \times 12$), and the cutting ends with a 12 mm square.

**Answer: (E) 12 mm**

prompt: In a soccer game the winner gains three points, while the loser gains zero points. If the game is a draw, then the two teams gain one point each. A team has played 38 games and gained 80 points. Find the greatest possible number of games that the team lost.

solutions.title: Win as often as possible
solutions.body:
To lose many games, the team should collect its 80 points in as few games as possible, so it should win as much as it can. 26 wins give 78 points, plus 2 draws = 80 points in 28 games. The other $38 - 28 = 10$ games were lost. (27 wins give 81, too many.)

**Answer: (C) 10**

solutions.title: Could it be 11?
solutions.body:
With 11 losses the 80 points come from 27 games. 27 wins give 81; changing a win into a draw takes 2 points away, giving 79, 77, ... — never 80. So 10 is the most.

**Answer: (C) 10**
